The number and authorship of this Psalm are stated (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.25">Ac 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">13:33</reference>). Though the warlike events of David's reign may have suggested its imagery, the scenes depicted and the subjects presented can only find a fulfilment in the history and character of Jesus Christ, to which, as above cited and in <reference osisRef="Heb.1.5">He 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">5:5</reference>, the New Testament writers most distinctly testify. In a most animated and highly poetical style, the writer, in "four stanzas of three verses each," sets forth the inveterate and furious, though futile, hostility of men to God and His anointed, God's determination to carry out His purpose, that purpose as stated more fully by His Son, the establishment of the Mediatorial kingdom, and the imminent danger of all who resist, as well as the blessing of all who welcome this mighty and triumphant king.</title> <div sID="gen8252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5461"/><hi type="bold">1. Why do the heathen, &c.--</hi>Beholding, in prophetic vision, the peoples and nations, as if in a tumultuous assembly, raging with a fury like the raging of the sea, designing to resist God's government, the writer breaks forth into an exclamation in which are mingled surprise at their folly, and indignation at their rebellion.<div eID="gen8252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heathen--</hi>nations generally, not as opposed to Jews.<div eID="gen8253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the people--</hi>or, literally, "peoples," or races of men. <div eID="gen8254" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: PSALM 2 Psa 2:1-12 . The number and authorship of this Psalm are stated ( Ac 4:25 ; 13:33 ). Though the warlike events of David's reign may have suggested its imagery, the scenes depicted and the subjects presented can only find a fulfilment in the history and character of Jesus Christ, to which, as above cited and in He 1:5 ; 5:5 , the New Testament writers most distinctly testify. In a most animated and highly poetical style, the writer, in "four stanzas of three verses each," sets forth the inveterate and furious, though futile, hostility of men to God and His anointed, God's determination to carry out His purpose, that purpose as stated more fully by His Son, the establishment of the Mediatorial kingdom, and the imminent danger of all who resist, as well as the blessing of all who welcome this mighty and triumphant king. 1. Why do the heathen, &c.-- Beholding, in prophetic vision, the peoples and nations, as if in a tumultuous assembly, raging with a fury like the raging of the sea, designing to resist God's government, the writer breaks forth into an exclamation in which are mingled surprise at their folly, and indignation at their rebellion. heathen-- nations generally, not as opposed to Jews. the people-- or, literally, "peoples," or races of men.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5462"/><div sID="gen8255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5462"/>2. The kings and rulers lead on their subjects.<div eID="gen8255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set themselves--</hi>take a stand.<div eID="gen8256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take counsel--</hi>literally, "sit together," denoting their deliberation.<div eID="gen8257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anointed--</hi>Hebrew, "Messiah"; Greek, "Christ" (<reference osisRef="John.1.41">Joh 1:41</reference>). Anointing, as an emblem of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, was conferred on prophets (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Is 6:1</reference>); priests (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.30">Ex 30:30</reference>); and kings (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1">1Sa 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">16:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.39">1Ki 1:39</reference>). Hence this title well suited Him who holds all these offices, and was generally used by the Jews before His coming, to denote Him (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>). While the prophet has in view men's opposition generally, he here depicts it in its culminating aspect as seen in the events of Christ's great trial. Pilate and Herod, and the rulers of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.1">Mt 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.1-Luke.23.25">Lu 23:1-25</reference>), with the furious mob, are vividly portrayed. <div eID="gen8258" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 2. The kings and rulers lead on their subjects. set themselves-- take a stand. take counsel-- literally, "sit together," denoting their deliberation. anointed-- Hebrew, "Messiah"; Greek, "Christ" ( Joh 1:41 ). Anointing, as an emblem of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, was conferred on prophets ( Is 6:1 ); priests ( Ex 30:30 ); and kings ( 1Sa 10:1 ; 16:13 ; 1Ki 1:39 ). Hence this title well suited Him who holds all these offices, and was generally used by the Jews before His coming, to denote Him ( Da 9:26 ). While the prophet has in view men's opposition generally, he here depicts it in its culminating aspect as seen in the events of Christ's great trial. Pilate and Herod, and the rulers of the Jews ( Mt 27:1 ; Lu 23:1-25 ), with the furious mob, are vividly portrayed.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5467"/><div sID="gen8271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5467"/>7. The king thus constituted declares the fundamental law of His kingdom, in the avowal of His Sonship, a relation involving His universal dominion.<div eID="gen8271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this day have I begotten thee--</hi>as <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2Sa 7:14</reference>, "he shall be My son," is a solemn recognition of this relation. The interpretation of this passage to describe the inauguration of Christ as Mediatorial King, by no means impugns the Eternal Sonship of His divine nature. In <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">Ac 13:33</reference>, Paul's quotation does not imply an application of this passage to the resurrection; for "raised up" in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.32">Ac 13:32</reference> is used as in <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>; 3:22, &c., to denote bringing Him into being as a man; and not that of resurrection, which it has only when, as in <reference osisRef="Acts.2.34">Ac 2:34</reference>, allusion is made to His death (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>). That passage says He was declared as to His divine nature to be the Son of God, by the resurrection, and only teaches that that event manifested a truth already existing. A similar recognition of His Sonship is introduced in <reference osisRef="Heb.5.5">He 5:5</reference>, by these ends, and by others in <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">17:5</reference>. <div eID="gen8272" type="x-p"/>

A similar recognition of His Sonship is introduced in He 5:5 , by these ends, and by others in Mt 3:17 ; 17:5 .
